decks.title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases — Part 1: organs, mechanism and volumes
goals: Name the respiratory organs of animals and label the human respiratory system
Explain inspiration and expiration in terms of volume and pressure
Define the pulmonary volumes and capacities and calculate them from a spirometer record

slides.heading: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
slides.body_md: Part 1: how air reaches the lungs and how much of it moves.

visual.alt: Flow of the path of air from the nostrils to the alveoli

slides.narration: Every cell needs oxygen and must get rid of carbon dioxide. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs, and gas exchange takes place across the thin walls of the alveoli. This part covers the organs of breathing, the mechanism of breathing and the volumes of air that move.

slides.heading: Respiratory organs in animals
slides.body_md: The organ depends on the size, habitat and activity of the animal.

rows: Network of tracheal tubes opening through spiracles
Moist skin, buccal cavity and lungs

visual.alt: Table of animal groups and their respiratory organs

slides.narration: Small and flat animals can simply let gases diffuse across the body surface. Insects carry air directly to tissues through tubes. Aquatic animals use gills, and land vertebrates use lungs. A frog uses all of skin, mouth lining and lungs.

slides.heading: Quick check: respiratory surfaces
slides.body_md: Decide which animal needs no special respiratory organ.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of a flat, thin animal with every cell close to the outside.

slides.heading: The human respiratory system
slides.body_md: Air passes **nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli**. The **right lung has three lobes** and the **left lung two**; each lung is wrapped in a **double-layered pleura** with fluid between the layers.

slides.narration: Follow the air from the nostrils to the alveoli. The nasal chamber filters, warms and moistens it. The larynx has the epiglottis, which covers the opening during swallowing. The trachea divides into two bronchi, one for each lung, and these branch again and again into bronchioles that end in alveoli.

slides.heading: Parts and their functions
slides.body_md: The system has a **conducting part** and an **exchange part**.

rows: Sound production; closes the windpipe during swallowing
Stays open; cilia sweep mucus and dust upward
Carry air into the lung lobes
Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Reduces friction as the lungs move

visual.alt: Table of parts of the respiratory system, their structure and function

slides.narration: The conducting part only carries air. Gas exchange happens only in the alveoli. The incomplete rings of cartilage keep the trachea open without pressing on the food pipe behind it, and the pleural fluid lets the lungs slide smoothly against the chest wall.

slides.heading: The mechanism of breathing
slides.body_md: Air moves because the **pressure in the lungs differs from the atmosphere**. The lungs lie in an air-tight chest, so when the chest changes volume the lungs change with it.

slides.narration: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs and the breastbone. The chest volume rises, the pressure in the lungs falls below the outside pressure, and air flows in. In expiration the muscles relax, the volume falls, the pressure rises, and air flows out.

slides.heading: Muscles used in breathing
slides.body_md: Quiet breathing uses little effort; deep breathing recruits more muscles.

rows: Passive recoil of the chest and lungs
The above plus extra muscles of the chest and neck
Takes in the inspiratory reserve volume

visual.alt: Table of muscles used in quiet and forced breathing

slides.narration: Quiet expiration needs no muscle work. It is simply the return of the stretched chest and lungs to their resting size. Only in deep or forced breathing do the internal intercostal and abdominal muscles help to push more air out.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: pressure and volume
slides.body_md: A student blocks her nose and mouth and tries to breathe in. The gas in her lungs expands from 2400 mL to 2450 mL while the temperature stays constant. The pressure was 760 mm Hg (atmospheric). Find the new pressure.
bullets: Use Boyle’s law for a fixed amount of gas: $p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2$.
The pressure falls by $760 - 744.5 = 15.5$ mm Hg, below atmospheric: if the airway were open, air would flow in.

visual.alt: Worked table: pressure falls from 760 to 744.5 millimetres of mercury

slides.narration: A bigger volume means a lower pressure, provided the amount of gas is fixed. With the airway blocked, the lungs cannot take in air, so the pressure falls. With the airway open, the fall in pressure is small, because air flows in at once and refills the lungs.

slides.heading: Volumes and capacities
slides.body_md: A **capacity** is the sum of two or more volumes.

rows: Air breathed in or out in one quiet breath
Extra air that can be breathed in after a quiet inspiration
Extra air that can be breathed out after a quiet expiration
Air left after the strongest expiration
IRV + TV + ERV: the largest air breathed out after a deep inspiration
ERV + RV: air left after a quiet expiration

visual.alt: Table of respiratory volumes and capacities with typical adult values

slides.narration: Learn the four volumes first. The capacities are sums. Vital capacity is the three measurable volumes added together. Add the residual volume to it and you have the total lung capacity. The residual volume is also part of the functional residual capacity.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: capacities from a record
slides.body_md: A spirometer test gives TV 450 mL, IRV 2400 mL, ERV 900 mL; the residual volume is 1050 mL. Find IC, EC, VC and TLC.
bullets: Inspiratory capacity $= \text{TV} + \text{IRV} = 450 + 2400 = 2850$ mL.
Expiratory capacity $= \text{TV} + \text{ERV} = 450 + 900 = 1350$ mL.
Vital capacity $= \text{IRV} + \text{TV} + \text{ERV} = 2400 + 450 + 900 = 3750$ mL.
Total lung capacity $= \text{VC} + \text{RV} = 3750 + 1050 = 4800$ mL.

visual.alt: Worked table: IC 2850, EC 1350, VC 3750, TLC 4800

slides.narration: Add the right volumes for each capacity. Inspiratory capacity is a quiet breath plus the inspiratory reserve. Vital capacity adds the expiratory reserve as well. Total lung capacity needs the residual volume, which only a special test can give.

slides.heading: Quick check: functional residual capacity
slides.body_md: Add the volumes that stay in the lungs after a quiet expiration.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which two volumes remain after a quiet breath out?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: ventilation
slides.body_md: Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume × breaths per minute. The conducting passages hold about 150 mL of air that never reaches the alveoli. Compare a girl breathing 14 times a minute with TV 450 mL, and a boy breathing 7 times a minute with TV 900 mL.
bullets: Girl: $450 \times 14 = 6300$ mL per minute; reaching the alveoli: $(450 - 150) \times 14 = 4200$ mL.
Boy: $900 \times 7 = 6300$ mL per minute; reaching the alveoli: $(900 - 150) \times 7 = 5250$ mL.
Same total, but **slow deep breathing** ventilates the alveoli better.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing shallow fast breathing and deep slow breathing

slides.narration: Both breathe the same total volume each minute. But in every breath the first one hundred and fifty millilitres only fill the air passages. The deep breather wastes this much only seven times a minute, so more fresh air reaches the alveoli.

slides.heading: Quick check: air reaching the alveoli
slides.body_md: Find the volume of fresh air reaching the alveoli each minute.
slides.narration: Quick check. Subtract the air in the air passages from each breath.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Organs: body surface, cuticle, tracheae, gills, skin and lungs; human lungs: three lobes right, two lobes left, pleura.
Inspiration: diaphragm and external intercostals contract, volume rises, pressure falls; expiration is passive in quiet breathing.
Volumes: TV, IRV, ERV, RV; capacities: IC, EC, FRC, VC, TLC.
VC = IRV + TV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV; FRC = ERV + RV.
Alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate.

visual.alt: Summary table of lung capacities and formulae

slides.narration: To recap: air flows because muscles change the volume of the chest and so the pressure in the lungs. The spirometer measures the volumes, and the capacities are their sums. The residual volume is the one volume it cannot measure.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say **pressure falls because volume rises**, never just "air is sucked in".
Write each capacity as a **sum of volumes**.
Label a diagram with **lines that touch the part**; name the right lung as three-lobed.
Remember that the **residual volume cannot be exhaled**, so the vital capacity excludes it.

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes and corrections

slides.narration: Exam tips. Link every movement of air to a change of volume and pressure. Write capacities as sums. Draw label lines carefully. And keep the residual volume out of the vital capacity.

slides.heading: Exchange, transport and control
slides.body_md: Part 2: how gases cross membranes, travel in blood and are regulated.

nodes.label: Carbon dioxide returns to the alveoli

visual.alt: Flow of gas exchange between alveoli, blood and tissues

slides.narration: Oxygen has to cross from the air in the alveoli into the blood, travel to the tissues and cross again into the cells. Carbon dioxide takes the opposite road. Gases move only by diffusion, so the whole story depends on differences in partial pressure.

slides.heading: Partial pressures and diffusion
slides.body_md: A gas diffuses from a region of **higher partial pressure** to one of **lower** partial pressure. The **diffusion membrane** (alveolar epithelium, capillary endothelium and the basement substance between them) is thinner than a millimetre.

visual.alt: Table of partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide at five sites

slides.narration: Oxygen moves from alveolar air into the blood because its partial pressure is higher in the air. Carbon dioxide moves the other way. Although its gradient is small, carbon dioxide is far more soluble than oxygen, so its diffusion is still quick. At the tissues the directions reverse.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: oxygen pressure and height
slides.body_md: Dry air is 20.9 percent oxygen at every height, but the **barometric pressure** falls as we climb, so the **partial pressure of oxygen** falls too: $p\mathrm{O_2} = 0.209 \times \text{barometric pressure}$.
bullets: Sea level: $0.209 \times 760 = 158.8$ mm Hg.
Hill town at about 2500 metres: $0.209 \times 560 = 117$ mm Hg.
Base camp at about 5500 metres: $0.209 \times 380 = 79.4$ mm Hg.
Summit at about 8800 metres: $0.209 \times 253 = 52.9$ mm Hg.

visual.alt: Worked table of oxygen partial pressure at four heights

slides.narration: The share of oxygen in air stays the same, but the whole air pressure drops with height. At the summit the partial pressure of oxygen is about one third of its sea level value, so the gradient into the blood is very small and climbers feel breathless.

slides.heading: Transport of oxygen
slides.body_md: Oxygen is carried by **haemoglobin** (Hb) in red cells. Each Hb molecule has four haem groups and can bind **four O₂ molecules**, forming **oxyhaemoglobin**.

visual.alt: Table of the forms in which oxygen is carried

slides.narration: Nearly all the oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin. Each molecule carries up to four oxygen molecules. Because the binding depends on the partial pressure of oxygen, haemoglobin loads oxygen in the lungs and unloads it in the tissues.

slides.heading: The oxygen dissociation curve
slides.body_md: A plot of **% saturation of Hb with O₂ against pO₂** is **sigmoid (S-shaped)**. The curve is flat near the lungs and steep near the tissues, so a small fall in pO₂ at the tissues releases a lot of oxygen.

slides.narration: At the lungs haemoglobin is nearly full. At the pressure found in resting tissues it is about three quarters full, so about a quarter of its load is released. The steep middle part of the curve is where small changes in pressure make large changes in saturation.

slides.heading: Factors that shift the curve
slides.body_md: In active tissues several factors help **haemoglobin release oxygen**: they shift the curve to the **right** (the **Bohr effect**).

visual.alt: Table of factors that shift the oxygen dissociation curve

slides.narration: Active muscle is warmer, more acidic and rich in carbon dioxide. All three move the curve to the right, so haemoglobin gives up more oxygen exactly where it is needed. In the lungs the opposite conditions favour loading.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much oxygen is delivered
slides.body_md: Blood has 15 g of haemoglobin in 100 mL, and 1 g binds 1.34 mL of oxygen. Arterial blood is 97 percent saturated and blood leaving resting tissue 75 percent. How much oxygen does 5000 mL of blood deliver?
bullets: Arterial blood: $15 \times 1.34 \times 97/100 \approx 19.5$ mL per 100 mL.
Venous blood: $15 \times 1.34 \times 75/100 \approx 15.1$ mL per 100 mL.

visual.alt: Worked table: 4.4 millilitres of oxygen given up per hundred millilitres

slides.narration: Multiply the haemoglobin mass by what each gram can bind and by the saturation. The difference between arterial and venous blood is what the tissues take up. Textbooks often round this to five millilitres per hundred millilitres of blood.

slides.narration: The enzyme carbonic anhydrase, found in red cells, makes carbon dioxide and water combine at once. The bicarbonate ions leave the cell, and chloride ions enter to keep the electrical balance. Haemoglobin takes up the hydrogen ions, which prevents the blood from becoming too acidic.

slides.heading: The three forms of carbon dioxide
slides.body_md: About **4 mL of CO₂** is delivered to the alveoli by each **100 mL of deoxygenated blood**. At the lungs the sequence reverses, and CO₂ diffuses into alveolar air.

rows: Mostly in plasma, formed inside red cells
CO₂ bound to Hb in red cells

visual.alt: Table of the three forms of carbon dioxide in blood

slides.narration: Most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate. About a quarter is carried by haemoglobin as carbamino compounds, which form more easily when haemoglobin has given up its oxygen. A small share is simply dissolved in plasma.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: sharing out carbon dioxide
slides.body_md: A resting person adds 230 mL of carbon dioxide to the blood each minute. Divide it among the three forms.
bullets: Bicarbonate: $70/100 \times 230 = 161$ mL.
Carbamino-haemoglobin: $23/100 \times 230 = 52.9$ mL.
Dissolved: $7/100 \times 230 = 16.1$ mL.

visual.alt: Worked table dividing carbon dioxide among its three forms

slides.narration: Multiply the total by each share. The three parts add back to the whole amount. The figure of twenty three percent is a mid value of the range given in textbooks.

slides.body_md: Name the ion that moves into the red cell.

slides.heading: Regulation of breathing
slides.body_md: Breathing is controlled by the **respiratory rhythm centre** in the **medulla**, helped by the **pneumotaxic centre** in the **pons** and a **chemosensitive area** next to the rhythm centre. **Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery** also sense CO₂ and H⁺.

nodes.label: Rise in CO₂ and H⁺ in blood
Chemosensitive area and aortic and carotid receptors

visual.alt: Flow of the regulation of breathing after a rise in carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions in the blood are the main signals. When they rise, the chemosensitive area and the receptors on the large arteries send signals to the rhythm centre. The pneumotaxic centre can shorten inspiration and so change the rate. Oxygen has only a minor role.

slides.heading: Respiratory disorders
slides.body_md: Breathing problems arise from the airways, the alveoli or inhaled dust.

rows: Inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles, often by an allergen
Damaged alveolar walls; cigarette smoking is a major cause
Fewer alveoli, less respiratory surface, breathlessness
Long exposure to dust from grinding, stone-breaking or asbestos
Inflammation and fibrosis of lung tissue

visual.alt: Table of respiratory disorders with causes and effects

slides.narration: In asthma the airways narrow and the person wheezes. In emphysema the walls between alveoli break down, so the surface for exchange shrinks. Workers in stone, mining and asbestos industries can develop fibrosis, which is why dust masks and ventilation are required.

slides.body_md: Decide what happens when a person re-breathes the same air.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which gas builds up in the blood?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Gases diffuse down partial-pressure gradients across the thin diffusion membrane.
Oxygen: about 97 percent as oxyhaemoglobin; the curve is sigmoid; higher pCO₂, acidity and temperature shift it right.
Carbon dioxide: about 70 percent bicarbonate, about 23 percent carbamino-haemoglobin, about 7 percent dissolved; carbonic anhydrase; chloride shift.
Breathing is controlled by the rhythm centre (medulla), the pneumotaxic centre (pons) and the chemosensitive area.
Asthma, emphysema and occupational disorders.

visual.alt: Summary table of oxygen and carbon dioxide transport

slides.narration: To recap: partial pressures drive diffusion in the lungs and tissues. Haemoglobin carries oxygen and releases it more freely in active tissues. Carbon dioxide is mainly carried as bicarbonate, and the chloride shift keeps the red cell balanced. Carbon dioxide level in the blood is the main drive to breathe.

sections.heading: 1. Respiratory organs in animals and the human respiratory system
sections.body_md:
**Respiration in animals (recall).** Animals take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide by different organs: **sponges, Hydra and flatworms** by simple diffusion across the general body surface; the **earthworm** through its moist cuticle; **insects** through a network of **tracheal tubes** that open by spiracles; **prawns and fishes** by **gills** (branchial respiration); **amphibians** such as the frog by moist skin, buccal cavity and lungs; **reptiles, birds and mammals** by **lungs** (pulmonary respiration).

**The human respiratory system** has a **conducting part** and an **exchange part**. Air enters through the **external nostrils** into the **nasal chamber**, whose hairs, mucus and rich blood supply filter, warm and moisten it. It then passes the **pharynx** (a common passage for food and air), the **larynx** (the cartilaginous sound box; the **epiglottis** covers the glottis during swallowing), the **trachea** (a straight tube, held open by **incomplete C-shaped cartilage rings**, lined by ciliated epithelium that sweeps mucus and dust upward), and the **right and left primary bronchi**. Each bronchus divides repeatedly into secondary and tertiary bronchi and **bronchioles**, ending in thin-walled, vascularised **alveoli**, the sites of gas exchange.

The **lungs** lie in the air-tight **thoracic chamber**, bounded dorsally by the vertebral column, ventrally by the sternum, laterally by the ribs and below by the **diaphragm**. Each lung is covered by a **double-layered pleura** enclosing a little pleural fluid, which reduces friction. The **right lung has three lobes** and the **left lung two**. The alveoli are so numerous that the exchange surface is far larger than the body surface; textbooks give different figures, so no figure is needed in answers.

**Drawing.** In a labelled diagram show nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx with epiglottis, trachea with rings, two bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, both lungs with lobes, and the diaphragm.

sections.heading: 2. Mechanism of breathing, pulmonary volumes and capacities
sections.body_md:
**Breathing** is the movement of air between the atmosphere and the alveoli, brought about by a difference in pressure. The lungs are in an air-tight chest, so a change in chest volume changes the volume of the lungs, and by **Boyle's law** (pressure falls as volume rises at constant temperature) the pressure inside them.

**Inspiration.** The **diaphragm contracts** and flattens, increasing the volume of the chest from top to bottom; the **external intercostal muscles contract**, lifting the ribs and sternum up and out and increasing the volume front to back. The **intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure** and air flows in. **Expiration.** The diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the diaphragm returns to its dome shape and the ribs and sternum fall; the volume decreases, the pressure rises above atmospheric and air flows out. Quiet expiration is passive. **Forced inspiration** uses extra muscles of the chest and neck; **forced expiration** uses the **internal intercostals and abdominal muscles**. A healthy adult breathes about 12 to 16 times a minute.

**Volumes and capacities** are measured with a **spirometer**:
- **Tidal volume (TV):** air breathed in or out in one quiet breath, about 500 mL.
- **Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV):** extra air that can be breathed in after a quiet inspiration, 2500 to 3000 mL.
- **Expiratory reserve volume (ERV):** extra air that can be breathed out after a quiet expiration, 1000 to 1100 mL.
- **Residual volume (RV):** air left in the lungs after the strongest expiration, 1100 to 1200 mL; it keeps the alveoli from collapsing and cannot be measured by simple spirometry.
- **Inspiratory capacity (IC)** = TV + IRV. **Expiratory capacity (EC)** = TV + ERV. **Functional residual capacity (FRC)** = ERV + RV. **Vital capacity (VC)** = IRV + TV + ERV (3500 to 4500 mL). **Total lung capacity (TLC)** = VC + RV (5000 to 6000 mL).

**Worked values.** For a student with TV 450, IRV 2400, ERV 900 and RV 1050 mL: IC = 2850, EC = 1350, FRC = 1950, VC = 3750 and TLC = 4800 mL.

**Ventilation.** Pulmonary ventilation = TV × breaths per minute. Air in the conducting passages (about 150 mL, the dead space) does not reach the alveoli, so alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate; slow deep breathing ventilates the alveoli better than fast shallow breathing.

key_terms.definition_md: Volume of air inspired or expired in one normal breath.
The maximum air that can be breathed out after a maximum inspiration: IRV + TV + ERV.
Volume of air that remains in the lungs after the strongest expiration.
ERV + RV: the air that stays in the lungs after a quiet expiration.

sections.heading: 3. Pulmonary exchange, transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide, chloride shift
sections.body_md:
**Exchange of gases** takes place at the alveoli and at the tissues by **simple diffusion**, driven by differences in **partial pressure** (pO₂, pCO₂). The **diffusion membrane** has three thin layers: the squamous epithelium of the alveoli, the endothelium of the alveolar capillaries and the basement substance between them, together thinner than a millimetre. Textbook values (mm Hg): atmospheric air pO₂ 159, pCO₂ 0.3; alveolar air 104 and 40; deoxygenated blood 40 and 45; oxygenated blood 95 and 40; tissues 40 and 45. The gradient for CO₂ is small, but CO₂ is **20 to 25 times more soluble** than O₂, so the amounts diffused are large. The partial pressure of oxygen in air is 0.209 times the barometric pressure, so it falls with height (sea level: 158.8 mm Hg; hill town at about 2500 metres: 117 mm Hg; base camp at about 5500 metres: 79.4 mm Hg; summit at about 8800 metres: 52.9 mm Hg).

**Transport of oxygen.** About **97 percent** is carried by **haemoglobin** in red cells as **oxyhaemoglobin**; about **3 percent** is dissolved in plasma. Each haemoglobin molecule can bind **four** oxygen molecules, and one gram of haemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen (this figure is from physiology texts, not the syllabus).

**The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve** is a plot of **percentage saturation of haemoglobin against pO₂**. It is **sigmoid**: nearly full saturation in the lungs (about 97 percent at pO₂ 100 mm Hg), about 75 percent at the pO₂ of resting tissue (40 mm Hg), so a quarter of the oxygen is released there. The curve **shifts to the right** (haemoglobin gives up oxygen more easily, the **Bohr effect**) with **higher pCO₂, higher H⁺ concentration (lower pH) and higher temperature**, as in active muscle; it shifts to the **left** with the opposite conditions, and with **foetal haemoglobin**, which takes oxygen from the mother's blood. The curves in this chapter are drawn from a standard formula for illustration (half-saturation at about 26.8, 33 and 20 mm Hg); books show similar curves.

**Transport of carbon dioxide.** About **70 percent** is carried as **bicarbonate ions**, about **20 to 25 percent** (here 23) as **carbamino-haemoglobin** and about **7 percent** dissolved in plasma. In the red cells at the tissues, the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** (also present in small amounts in plasma) speeds the reaction CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Haemoglobin buffers the H⁺. HCO₃⁻ diffuses out into plasma, and **Cl⁻ moves into the red cell** to keep it electrically neutral: the **chloride shift** (Hamburger shift). At the alveoli the reactions reverse and CO₂ diffuses out. Each 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂ to the alveoli.

The shift of the dissociation curve to the right by higher pCO₂, acidity or temperature, so that more oxygen is released.

sections.heading: 4. Regulation of breathing and respiratory disorders
sections.body_md:
**Regulation.** The rhythm of breathing is set by the **respiratory rhythm centre** in the **medulla oblongata**. The **pneumotaxic centre** in the **pons** moderates it: it can reduce the duration of inspiration and so alter the rate. A **chemosensitive area**, close to the rhythm centre, is highly sensitive to **CO₂ and hydrogen ions**; an increase in either activates the centre to make a change that eliminates them (faster, deeper breathing). **Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery** also recognise changes in CO₂ and H⁺ and send signals to the rhythm centre. The role of oxygen in regulation is quite insignificant in health. Breathing can be held voluntarily for a short time, but rising CO₂ eventually forces a breath.

**Respiratory disorders.**
- **Asthma:** difficulty in breathing causing wheezing, due to **inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles**, often triggered by an allergen such as pollen or dust.
- **Emphysema:** a chronic disorder in which the **alveolar walls are damaged**, decreasing the respiratory surface; **cigarette smoking** is a major cause. Breathlessness and a barrel-shaped chest are common signs.
- **Occupational respiratory disorders:** long exposure to dust in industries such as grinding or stone-breaking (**silicosis**, from silica), **asbestosis** (asbestos fibre) and coal-mining lung disease cause inflammation and **fibrosis** of the upper parts of the lungs. Workers should wear protective masks and the workplace should be ventilated. Books name different examples, and the syllabus asks only for the cause and symptoms of such disorders.

key_terms.definition_md: A centre in the medulla that sets the rhythm of breathing.
A centre in the pons that moderates the rhythm centre by reducing the duration of inspiration.
An area near the rhythm centre that is sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺.
A disorder in which damaged alveolar walls reduce the respiratory surface.
Inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles causing wheezing and difficulty in breathing.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying air is "sucked in" without stating that the volume rises and the pressure falls.
- Including the residual volume in the vital capacity, or leaving it out of the total lung capacity.
- Saying that quiet expiration needs muscle contraction.
- Writing that chloride ions leave the red cell with bicarbonate (they enter).
- Giving only the shape of the dissociation curve and not the cause and direction of a shift.
- Confusing asthma (airways) with emphysema (alveoli).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a definition, a term, a location, a give-a-reason, a sum of volumes.
- 2–3-mark questions: inspiration and expiration, volumes from a record, the chloride shift, factors shifting the curve, the three respiratory centres.
- 5-mark questions in parts: a labelled diagram of the respiratory system; capacities from a spirometer tracing; transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide; regulation and disorders.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The right lung of a human has two lobes and the left lung has three lobes.
questions.solution_md: False. The right lung has three lobes and the left lung two, because the heart takes up room on the left side.

questions.stem_md: The air-tight thoracic chamber is bounded dorsally by the vertebral column, laterally by the ribs, below by the diaphragm and ventrally by the ______.
questions.solution_md: The sternum forms the ventral boundary.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The trachea does not collapse when the air pressure inside it falls during inspiration.

answer.model_answer_md: Its wall is supported by **incomplete C-shaped rings of cartilage**, which keep the tube open.

questions.solution_md: Cartilage rings.

marking_scheme.step: Cartilage rings hold the tube open

questions.stem_md: Mention three ways in which the nasal chamber prepares air before it reaches the lungs.

answer.model_answer_md: Hairs and **mucus** in the nasal chamber **filter** out dust and germs; the rich **blood supply** under the lining **warms** the air; and the moist lining **moistens** it. The air reaching the lungs is therefore clean, warm and humid.

questions.solution_md: Filter, warm, moisten.

questions.stem_md: Name the respiratory organ or surface of (i) an earthworm, (ii) a cockroach, (iii) a prawn, (iv) a frog and (v) a rat, and name one more animal that breathes in the same way as the prawn.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The earthworm breathes through its **moist cuticle (skin)**. (ii) The cockroach has **tracheal tubes** opening through spiracles. (iii) The prawn breathes with **gills (branchiae)**, as **fishes** do. (iv) The frog uses **moist skin, the buccal cavity and lungs**. (v) The rat, a mammal, breathes with **lungs**.

questions.solution_md: Five organs and one more gill-breather.

marking_scheme.step: Gills of the prawn; fish as the other animal
Frog (skin, buccal cavity, lungs) and rat (lungs)

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a neat labelled diagram of the human respiratory system, showing the nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, both lungs and the diaphragm. [3]
(b) Describe two features of the alveoli that make them suitable for gas exchange. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The diagram shows the **nasal chamber** leading to the **pharynx** and the **larynx**, then the **trachea**, which divides into the **right and left bronchi**. The **right lung (three lobes)** and **left lung (two lobes)** lie in the chest, each with branching **bronchioles** ending in **alveoli**, and the dome of the **diaphragm** lies below the lungs. Label lines must touch the parts, and the trachea should show cartilage rings.

(b) The wall of an alveolus is **one cell thick**, so the diffusion distance is very short. Each alveolus is **wrapped by a network of capillaries**, which carry gases to and from the blood. (The very large number of alveoli gives a large surface area.)

questions.solution_md: Diagram with labels; two alveolar features.

Which statement is correct?

The balloons represent the diaphragm, and they inflate because the pressure in the jar rises.
The rubber sheet represents the diaphragm, the jar represents the chest, and pulling the sheet lowers the pressure around the balloons so that air enters them.

questions.solution_md: Pulling the sheet down enlarges the jar like a contracting diaphragm; the pressure in the jar falls below atmospheric and air flows into the balloons (lungs) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A trumpet player takes a deep breath and then blows out as much air as possible. Which muscles contract in addition to those used in quiet breathing during this forced expiration?

options.text_md: Internal intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles
External intercostal muscles and the diaphragm only
Only the muscles of the neck

questions.solution_md: Forced expiration is active: internal intercostals pull the ribs down and abdominal muscles push the diaphragm up — option (a).

questions.solution_md: When no air is moving through an open airway, the pressure inside the lungs has equalised with the pressure outside — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a part of the vital capacity?
questions.solution_md: Vital capacity is IRV + TV + ERV; the residual volume remains in the lungs even after the strongest expiration — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Some air always stays in the lungs even after the strongest possible expiration, and this keeps the alveoli from collapsing. This air is the
questions.solution_md: The air left after the strongest expiration is the residual volume — option (c).

questions.solution_md: The vital capacity is the whole range from the lowest level after a maximum expiration to the highest level after a maximum inspiration: bracket E — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each respiratory volume in column I with its description in column II.

match_right.text_md: Extra air breathed out after a quiet expiration
Largest volume breathed out after a maximum inspiration
Extra air breathed in after a quiet inspiration
Air left in the lungs after the strongest expiration

questions.solution_md: IRV is the extra air breathed in; ERV the extra breathed out; RV the air that cannot be expelled; VC the maximum breathed out after a maximum breath in.

questions.stem_md: A student's expiratory reserve volume is 900 mL and her residual volume is 1050 mL. What is her functional residual capacity in mL?
questions.solution_md: FRC $= \text{ERV} + \text{RV} = 900 + 1050 = 1950$ mL.

questions.stem_md: A boy breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 600 mL. If the air in his conducting passages (dead space) is 150 mL, how many mL of fresh air reach his alveoli each minute?
questions.solution_md: Fresh air per breath $= 600 - 150 = 450$ mL; per minute $= 450 \times 12 = 5400$ mL.

questions.stem_md: The inspiratory capacity of a boy is 3100 mL and his expiratory reserve volume is 1050 mL. Calculate his vital capacity in mL.
questions.solution_md: IC already contains TV and IRV, so $\text{VC} = \text{IC} + \text{ERV} = 3100 + 1050 = 4150$ mL.

questions.stem_md: For the student in the spirometer record (TV 450 mL, IRV 2400 mL, ERV 900 mL, RV 1050 mL), what percentage of the total lung capacity is the residual volume? Give the answer to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: TLC $= 2400 + 450 + 900 + 1050 = 4800$ mL; $\dfrac{1050}{4800} \times 100 = 21.875$, which is 21.9 percent to one decimal place.

questions.stem_md: Before a deep breath, the gas in a person's lungs has a volume of 2500 mL at 760 mm Hg. Suppose the airway is blocked and the chest then enlarges so that the gas occupies 2560 mL at the same temperature. Calculate the new pressure in mm Hg, to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: Boyle's law: $p_2 = \dfrac{p_1 V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{760 \times 2500}{2560} \approx 742.2$ mm Hg, lower than atmospheric pressure.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The total lung capacity of a person is always greater than the vital capacity.

**Reason (R):** Some air, the residual volume, remains in the lungs even after the strongest expiration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true: TLC = VC + RV, so the air that cannot be expelled makes TLC larger than VC — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Explain how the contraction of the diaphragm leads to air entering the lungs. Answer in terms of volume and pressure.

answer.model_answer_md: When the diaphragm **contracts**, it flattens and the **volume of the thoracic chamber increases**. The lungs expand with the chest, so the **pressure inside them falls below the atmospheric pressure**. Air therefore flows from outside, where the pressure is higher, into the lungs.

questions.solution_md: Volume up, pressure down, air flows in.

marking_scheme.step: Flattening increases the volume of the chest and the lungs
Pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in

questions.stem_md: Why is quiet expiration called a passive process? Name the muscles that make forced expiration active.

answer.model_answer_md: In quiet expiration the muscles of inspiration simply **relax**, and the **elastic recoil** of the chest and lungs reduces the volume and raises the pressure, so no muscle work is needed. **Forced expiration** is active because the **internal intercostal muscles** and the **abdominal muscles** contract.

questions.solution_md: Relaxation and recoil; internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

marking_scheme.step: Muscles relax and recoil expels air, so passive
Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles in forced expiration

questions.stem_md: Define vital capacity and state how it is calculated from the respiratory volumes.

answer.model_answer_md: **Vital capacity** is the **maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a maximum inspiration**. It is calculated as the **sum of the inspiratory reserve volume, the tidal volume and the expiratory reserve volume**; the residual volume is not included.

questions.solution_md: Definition; IRV + TV + ERV.

questions.stem_md: Describe the sequence of events in quiet inspiration, starting with the muscles, and say how each change leads to air entering the lungs.

answer.model_answer_md: The **diaphragm contracts and flattens**, and the **external intercostal muscles contract**, lifting the ribs and the sternum up and outward. The **volume of the thoracic chamber increases** in both the vertical and the front-to-back directions. The lungs, held against the chest wall by the pleura, expand, so the **intra-pulmonary pressure falls below the atmospheric pressure** and **air flows in** until the pressures are equal.

questions.solution_md: Muscles; volume; pressure and flow.

marking_scheme.step: Diaphragm flattens and external intercostals lift the ribs and sternum
Volume of the chest and lungs increases
Pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in

questions.stem_md: A spirometer record of a student gives a tidal volume of 520 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 2650 mL and an expiratory reserve volume of 1150 mL. Calculate her vital capacity. Explain why her total lung capacity cannot be found from these three readings alone.

answer.model_answer_md:
Vital capacity $= \text{IRV} + \text{TV} + \text{ERV} = 2650 + 520 + 1150 = 4320$ mL.

Total lung capacity is the vital capacity **plus the residual volume**. The residual volume is the air that **stays in the lungs after the strongest expiration**, so it never leaves the lungs and **cannot be recorded by a spirometer** that measures only air moving in and out of the mouth.

questions.solution_md: VC; reason for the missing RV.

marking_scheme.step: Vital capacity as the sum of three volumes
TLC needs the residual volume, which a spirometer cannot record

questions.stem_md:
A trained swimmer's spirometer record gives: tidal volume 600 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 3300 mL, expiratory reserve volume 1300 mL; the residual volume measured separately is 1400 mL.
(a) Calculate the inspiratory capacity and the expiratory capacity. [2]
(b) Calculate the vital capacity and the total lung capacity. [2]
(c) Calculate the functional residual capacity and say what it represents. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) IC $= \text{TV} + \text{IRV} = 600 + 3300 = 3900$ mL; EC $= \text{TV} + \text{ERV} = 600 + 1300 = 1900$ mL.

(b) VC $= \text{IRV} + \text{TV} + \text{ERV} = 3300 + 600 + 1300 = 5200$ mL; TLC $= \text{VC} + \text{RV} = 5200 + 1400 = 6600$ mL.

(c) FRC $= \text{ERV} + \text{RV} = 1300 + 1400 = 2700$ mL; it is the **volume of air that remains in the lungs after a quiet (normal) expiration**.

questions.solution_md: Capacities as sums of volumes.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain the mechanism of normal inspiration, naming the muscles involved and the changes in volume and pressure. [3]
(b) How does expiration differ from inspiration in a person at rest? [1]
(c) Name two muscle groups that make forced expiration possible. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **diaphragm contracts and flattens**, and the **external intercostals contract**, raising the ribs and sternum. The **volume of the thoracic chamber rises**, so the **pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure** and air flows in.

(b) In quiet expiration the muscles **relax** and the elastic recoil of the chest and lungs reduces the volume and raises the pressure, so it is **passive**, whereas inspiration is active.

(c) **Internal intercostal muscles** and **abdominal muscles**.

questions.solution_md: Inspiration; passive expiration; forced expiration.

questions.stem_md: In the capillaries of a resting muscle, the pO₂ of the surrounding tissue is 40 mm Hg and its pCO₂ is 45 mm Hg, while the blood arriving there has pO₂ 95 mm Hg and pCO₂ 40 mm Hg. In which directions do the gases diffuse?

options.text_md: Oxygen from the tissue into the blood, and carbon dioxide from the blood into the tissue
Both gases from the blood into the tissue
Oxygen from the blood into the tissue, and carbon dioxide from the tissue into the blood
Both gases from the tissue into the blood

questions.solution_md: Each gas moves from higher to lower partial pressure: oxygen 95 to 40, carbon dioxide 45 to 40 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: What is the maximum number of oxygen molecules that one molecule of haemoglobin can carry?
questions.solution_md: Haemoglobin has four haem groups, each able to bind one oxygen molecule — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A patient with a high fever has a body temperature of 40 °C instead of the usual 37 °C. Compared with its behaviour at normal temperature, how does her haemoglobin behave at the tissues?

options.text_md: It holds oxygen more tightly, because the curve shifts to the left
It releases the same amount, because temperature has no effect
It releases oxygen more readily, because the curve shifts to the right
It cannot bind oxygen at all

questions.solution_md: A rise in temperature shifts the dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin gives up oxygen more readily — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the figure, the dot on curve C is at a pO₂ of 40 mm Hg, the value in resting tissue. About what percentage of the haemoglobin is saturated with oxygen at the dot?
questions.solution_md: The standard curve passes through about 75 percent saturation at 40 mm Hg — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a tissue capillary, bicarbonate ions diffuse out of the red blood cells into the plasma. Which ion moves into the red blood cells at the same time, so that the cells stay electrically neutral?
questions.solution_md: Chloride ions enter the red cells as bicarbonate ions leave: the chloride shift — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Blood from the tissues reaches the alveolar capillaries. Which change takes place inside its red blood cells?

options.text_md: Carbon dioxide is converted to bicarbonate ions
Chloride ions leave the cells as carbon dioxide enters them
Bicarbonate ions enter the cells and are converted back to carbon dioxide and water

questions.solution_md: At the alveoli the lower pCO₂ reverses the reactions: bicarbonate enters the cells and carbonic anhydrase helps to form CO₂, which diffuses out — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On the standard curve, haemoglobin is 97 percent saturated at a pO₂ of 100 mm Hg and 75 percent saturated at 40 mm Hg. What fraction of its oxygen load does the haemoglobin release as blood passes through a resting tissue?
questions.solution_md: $(97 - 75)/97 \approx 0.23$: about one quarter — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Most of the oxygen in the blood is carried dissolved in the plasma.
questions.solution_md: False. About 97 percent of the oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in the red cells; only about 3 percent is dissolved in plasma.

questions.stem_md: The enzyme ______, present in large amounts in red blood cells, speeds up the combination of carbon dioxide with water.
questions.solution_md: Carbonic anhydrase.

questions.stem_md: A woman has 13 g of haemoglobin in every 100 mL of blood. One gram of haemoglobin can bind 1.34 mL of oxygen, and her arterial blood is 98 percent saturated. How many mL of oxygen does 100 mL of her arterial blood carry on haemoglobin? Give one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: $13 \times 1.34 \times 98/100 \approx 17.1$ mL.

questions.stem_md: For the woman above, venous blood leaving her resting muscles is 70 percent saturated (12.2 mL of oxygen per 100 mL) and arterial blood carries 17.1 mL per 100 mL. If 4800 mL of blood flows through her tissues each minute, how many mL of oxygen are delivered per minute? Give one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: Given up per 100 mL $= 17.1 - 12.2 = 4.9$ mL; per minute $= 4.9 \times 4800/100 = 235.2$ mL.

questions.stem_md: At a mountain pass the barometric pressure is 480 mm Hg. Taking oxygen to be 20.9 percent of dry air, calculate the partial pressure of oxygen there in mm Hg, to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: $0.209 \times 480 \approx 100.3$ mm Hg.

questions.stem_md: A person at rest adds 250 mL of carbon dioxide to the blood every minute. If about 70 percent of it is carried as bicarbonate ions, how many mL per minute is carried in that form?
questions.solution_md: $70/100 \times 250 = 175$ mL per minute.

questions.stem_md: Haemoglobin is 97 percent saturated at the lungs and 75 percent saturated in resting tissue. What percentage of the oxygen it carried to the tissue does it release there? Give one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: $(97 - 75)/97 \times 100 \approx 22.7$ percent.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the solubility of the gas is not the reason: carbonic anhydrase in the red cells converts CO₂ rapidly to bicarbonate, and the chloride shift removes it — option (b).

answer.model_answer_md: Bicarbonate ions **diffuse out** of the red cells, and chloride ions enter to **keep the cell electrically neutral** (the chloride shift).

questions.stem_md: What is the oxygen dissociation curve? State its shape and explain why the curve is steep at the pO₂ of the tissues but flat at the pO₂ of the lungs.

answer.model_answer_md: It is the plot of the **percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen against the pO₂**, and it is **sigmoid (S-shaped)**. At the high pO₂ of the lungs the curve is **flat**, because haemoglobin is almost fully saturated. At the lower pO₂ of the tissues the curve is **steep**, so a small fall in pO₂ releases a lot of oxygen.

questions.solution_md: Definition and shape; flat and steep parts.

marking_scheme.step: Flat at the lungs, steep at the tissues, with reason

questions.stem_md: What is the chloride shift? Name the enzyme that helps to produce the ions involved.

answer.model_answer_md: In a tissue capillary, carbon dioxide forms **bicarbonate ions** in the red cell and these **diffuse out** into the plasma. **Chloride ions move into the cell** to keep it electrically balanced: this exchange is the **chloride shift** (Hamburger shift). The ions are produced with the help of the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase**.

questions.solution_md: Cl⁻ enters as HCO₃⁻ leaves; carbonic anhydrase.

marking_scheme.step: Chloride moves in as bicarbonate moves out

questions.solution_md: Three forms and shares.

questions.stem_md: Name three conditions in a working muscle that shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, and explain how the shift helps the muscle.

answer.model_answer_md: The three conditions are a **higher pCO₂**, a **higher hydrogen ion concentration (lower pH)** and a **higher temperature**. They shift the curve to the **right**, so at the same pO₂ the haemoglobin is **less saturated**: it **releases more oxygen** to the muscle exactly where the demand for oxygen has risen.

questions.solution_md: Three factors; effect.

questions.stem_md: Compare the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood, giving the main form in which each is carried and the approximate percentages.

answer.model_answer_md: **Oxygen:** about **97 percent** is carried as **oxyhaemoglobin** in the red cells and about **3 percent** is dissolved in plasma. **Carbon dioxide:** about **70 percent** is carried as **bicarbonate ions**, about **20 to 25 percent** as **carbamino-haemoglobin** and about **7 percent** dissolved in plasma. Haemoglobin therefore has a major role in both gases, and the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** is needed only for the carbon dioxide.

questions.solution_md: Oxygen forms; carbon dioxide forms; enzyme.

marking_scheme.step: Carbon dioxide: bicarbonate 70, carbamino 20 to 25, dissolved 7

questions.stem_md: The pO₂ and pCO₂ of the blood arriving at a resting muscle are 95 and 40 mm Hg, while those of the muscle tissue are 40 and 45 mm Hg. Find the partial-pressure difference for each gas and state the direction in which each gas diffuses.

answer.model_answer_md: **Oxygen:** the difference is $95 - 40 = 55$ mm Hg, and oxygen diffuses from the **blood into the tissue**, where its pressure is lower. **Carbon dioxide:** the difference is $45 - 40 = 5$ mm Hg, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the **tissue into the blood**. Each gas moves from higher to lower partial pressure.

questions.solution_md: Gradients and directions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the forms in which oxygen is carried in the blood, with percentages. [1]
(b) Describe the shape of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve and what it shows about loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues. [2]
(c) State two factors that shift the curve to the right and explain the effect of the shift. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) About **97 percent** is carried as **oxyhaemoglobin** and about **3 percent** is dissolved in plasma.

(b) The curve is **sigmoid**. It is **flat at the high pO₂ of the lungs**, so haemoglobin is almost fully saturated there (loading); it is **steep at the lower pO₂ of the tissues**, so a small fall in pO₂ releases much oxygen (unloading).

(c) A **higher pCO₂**, **higher H⁺ concentration (lower pH)** or **higher temperature** shifts the curve to the **right**; haemoglobin is then less saturated at the same pO₂, so it **gives up more oxygen**.

questions.solution_md: Forms; curve; shifts.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a red blood cell in a tissue capillary showing how carbon dioxide is converted to bicarbonate ions and how the chloride shift occurs. [3]
(b) State the forms in which carbon dioxide is carried, with approximate percentages. [1]
(c) What happens to the bicarbonate ions at the lungs? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The diagram shows **CO₂ entering the red cell** from the tissues; **carbonic anhydrase** converting CO₂ + H₂O into **H₂CO₃**, which splits into **H⁺ and HCO₃⁻**; **H⁺ taken up by haemoglobin**; some **CO₂ bound to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin**; **HCO₃⁻ leaving** into the plasma and **Cl⁻ entering** the cell (chloride shift).

(b) About **70 percent as bicarbonate**, **20 to 25 percent as carbamino-haemoglobin** and about **7 percent dissolved** in plasma.

(c) At the lungs the reactions **reverse**: bicarbonate re-enters the red cells and, with carbonic anhydrase, forms **CO₂ and water**; the CO₂ **diffuses out into the alveoli**.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; forms; reversal.

marking_scheme.step: (a) CO₂ entry and carbonic anhydrase reaction

**(c)** (i) The **respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla**, helped by the **chemosensitive area** and by receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery, increases the rate and depth of breathing in response to a **rise in carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion concentration** of the blood.

questions.stem_md: A child breathes in and out of a closed paper bag for a minute. Her breathing becomes faster and deeper. What is the main reason?

options.text_md: The oxygen concentration of the bag is too high
The pneumotaxic centre is damaged by the paper
Her diaphragm becomes unable to contract
The carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion concentrations of her blood rise and stimulate the chemosensitive area

questions.solution_md: Re-breathing the same air raises the CO₂ and H⁺ of the blood, which stimulates the chemosensitive area and the rhythm centre — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In an experiment, an animal’s pneumotaxic centre is destroyed, while its respiratory rhythm centre remains intact. What is the likely effect on its breathing?

options.text_md: Inspiration is shortened and the rate rises sharply
There is no change at all
Inspiration lasts longer, so breaths become slower and deeper

questions.solution_md: The pneumotaxic centre moderates the rhythm centre by shortening inspiration; without it the inspiration is prolonged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A child with asthma is given an inhaler during an attack. It relieves the wheezing because it

options.text_md: removes fibrous tissue from the lungs
relaxes the muscles of the bronchioles and widens the air passages
increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood

questions.solution_md: Asthma narrows the bronchi and bronchioles by inflammation and muscle contraction; a bronchodilator widens them — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Compared with a healthy non-smoker, the lungs of a long-term heavy smoker with emphysema have

options.text_md: broken alveolar walls and a reduced respiratory surface
thickened bronchi and an increased respiratory surface
fibrous tissue caused by silica dust
more alveoli and a thinner diffusion membrane

questions.solution_md: Emphysema is the damage of alveolar walls, which reduces the surface for gas exchange — option (a).

options.text_md: asthma caused by an allergy to pollen
an occupational respiratory disorder caused by inhaled fibres

questions.stem_md: Describe the sequence of events by which a rise of carbon dioxide in the blood changes the rhythm of breathing. Name the sensors and the centres involved.

answer.model_answer_md: A rise in **CO₂ and H⁺** is detected by the **chemosensitive area** next to the rhythm centre and by receptors in the **aortic arch and carotid artery**. questions.stem_md: Distinguish between emphysema and an occupational lung disorder such as silicosis, with reference to the cause, the tissue affected and one symptom of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Emphysema** is caused mainly by **cigarette smoking**; the **alveolar walls are damaged**, the respiratory surface falls and the patient is breathless. **Silicosis** is caused by long exposure to **silica dust** in grinding or stone-breaking work; the **lung tissue becomes inflamed and fibrous** (fibrosis), and the patient coughs and has difficulty in breathing.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why can a person hold the breath voluntarily for only a short time? [2]
(b) State the location and function of the respiratory rhythm centre and of the pneumotaxic centre. [2]
(c) Which part of the brain would you expect to be affected if a person’s breathing stopped suddenly after a head injury? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) While the breath is held, **carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions accumulate** in the blood. They stimulate the **chemosensitive area** and the receptors on the large arteries, and the **rhythm centre** soon overrides the voluntary control and forces a breath.

(b) The **respiratory rhythm centre** lies in the **medulla oblongata** and sets the rhythm of breathing. The **pneumotaxic centre** lies in the **pons** and **moderates the rhythm centre** by shortening inspiration and so changing the rate.

(c) The **medulla oblongata**, which contains the respiratory rhythm centre.

questions.solution_md: CO₂ build-up; two centres; medulla.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is asthma? State its cause and one symptom. [2]
(b) How does emphysema reduce the efficiency of gas exchange? [2]
(c) Name one occupational respiratory disorder and one precaution against it. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Asthma is a disorder in which the **bronchi and bronchioles become inflamed**, usually in response to an **allergen**; the main symptoms are **wheezing** and **difficulty in breathing**.

(b) In emphysema the **alveolar walls are damaged**, so the **respiratory surface decreases**; less oxygen enters the blood and the patient is breathless. Cigarette smoking is a major cause.

(c) **Silicosis** (or asbestosis) caused by dust; workers should **wear protective masks** and the workplace should be well ventilated.

questions.solution_md: Asthma; emphysema; occupational disorder.

(b) Damaged alveolar walls and reduced surface

Mr Kulkarni, aged 64, smoked for forty years and is now breathless on climbing a few stairs. A lung-function report compares him with a healthy man of the same height.

| | Mr Kulkarni | Healthy man |
|---|---|---|
| Vital capacity (mL) | 2400 | 4000 |
